items.title: Britain's climate is anomalously warm for its latitude
items.claim: London sits at 51 degrees North — the same latitude as Calgary, Canada (winters of -30 C). Why is London so much warmer?

options.text: The Gulf Stream and the wider North Atlantic Current transport tropical heat northward, with prevailing westerlies carrying it onshore
The North Sea acts as a giant heat reservoir from summer
Britain receives more solar radiation due to cloud cover patterns
The Jet Stream alone is responsible

items.reveal:
The Gulf Stream originates in the Gulf of Mexico, feeds the North Atlantic Current, and as it cools and becomes saltier, sinks near Iceland and Greenland — driving the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). The energy transfer is roughly 1.3 petawatts, about 10,000 times UK electricity demand.

The AMOC has weakened measurably since the mid-20th century. A collapse would cool Britain dramatically while warming the tropics — a non-linear climate flip.
items.why: Climate is not just latitude. Ocean circulation is one of the largest energy-redistribution systems on the planet, and it's not guaranteed to keep running.

items.title: The Amazon generates much of its own rainfall
items.claim: How much of South American rainfall depends on Amazon transpiration?

options.text: None — rainfall comes entirely from the Atlantic

Amazon trees transpire huge volumes of water vapour, recycling moisture 5-6 times across the basin and generating 'flying rivers' that supply rainfall to southeast South America — including Brazil's agricultural heartland

items.reveal:
A mature Amazon tree can transpire 200-1,000 litres per day. The 'flying river' concept, popularised through INPE (Brazilian space agency) research and Antonio Nobre's work, describes the moisture flux from the basin southward — equivalent to or exceeding the Amazon River's surface discharge.

Deforestation reduces transpiration. Gatti et al. (Nature 2021) showed that the southern and eastern Amazon are already becoming net carbon sources. A tipping point at around 20-25% deforestation could shift large parts of the forest to savannah — with major consequences for Brazilian rainfall and agriculture.

Current deforestation is around 17-20% of the original Amazon area.
items.why: Forests are climate machines. Amazon loss would change rainfall patterns far beyond the basin — and threaten the agricultural economy that has driven much of the deforestation in the first place.

items.title: Tokyo is the world's largest urban area at around 37 million
items.claim: How many megacities exist and which is largest?

options.text: Around 33 megacities (cities over 10 million inhabitants) as of 2022; Tokyo is largest at around 37 million, followed by Delhi (32 m), Shanghai (28 m), Dhaka (23 m), São Paulo (22 m)

items.reveal:
UN World Urbanization Prospects (2018, updated 2022) lists 33 megacities. Largest by metropolitan area: Tokyo (37 m), Delhi (32 m), Shanghai (28 m), Dhaka (23 m), São Paulo (22 m), Cairo (22 m), Mexico City (22 m), Beijing (21 m), Mumbai (21 m), Osaka (19 m).

Lagos (Nigeria, around 15 m) is the fastest growing — UN projections suggest it could exceed 30 m by 2050. By 2050, around 50 megacities are projected, most in Africa and South Asia.

Definitions matter: 'city proper' versus 'urban agglomeration' versus 'metropolitan area' produce different rankings.
items.why: The geography of global population has shifted. 19th-century urban hierarchies (London, Paris, New York) no longer describe reality. The major cities of the 21st century are largely in countries that were poor a generation ago.
